I've gathered material from several key sources. Let me now compile verse-by-verse notes, noting where I could and couldn't find certain views.

---

# Psalm 58 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Superscription: "Do Not Destroy… A Miktam of David"

- **"Do Not Destroy" (Al-taschith):** Possibly the tune name, or a reference to David's determination not to destroy Saul (1 Samuel 24, 26), or David's plea that God would not allow him to be destroyed (Enduring Word / Guzik). Spurgeon notes: "The wicked are here judged and condemned, but over the godly the sacred 'Destroy not' is solemnly pronounced." — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps058.php
- **"Miktam":** Often taken to mean "golden" (a golden psalm), or from a root meaning "to engrave," possibly suggesting David inscribed these psalms on cave walls while in hiding (Jebb, cited by Spurgeon). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- **Occasion:** Gill surveys several views: when Saul threatened the priests for not revealing David's location (Syriac); the Nabal incident (Lightfoot); David in Saul's trench (Jarchi); or concerning Abner and Saul's princes who judged David a rebel (Kimchi). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm

---

## v. 1 — "Do you indeed speak justly, O rulers?"

- **The addressees:** Most older commentators agree these are unjust judges or rulers. The Hebrew word *elem* is debated. The Pulpit Commentary says rendering it "congregation" (KJV) is "contrary to all analogy, and quite untenable." It must mean "dumb ones" (silent ones) or be a corruption of *elim* ("mighty ones"). In either case it refers to judges, not the congregation. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm
- Bible.org notes the MT has a term that could relate to "silence" or "mighty lords." It must parallel "sons of men," so it refers to civic leaders/judges, not gods (cf. Psalm 82; Exod 22:8-9). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-58
- **"Silent ones":** Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/charismatic) says David challenged leaders who should have defended innocents but instead stayed silent. "The interrogation… expresses wonder, as at something scarcely credible. Can it be so? … Are you really silent, you, whose very office is to speak for God?" (Alexander, cited in Spurgeon). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- **Irony:** Both the Pulpit Commentary and Gill agree the questions are asked in bitter irony — these rulers do *not* speak righteousness or judge uprightly. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm
- Gill notes David calls them "sons of men" to remind them of their frailty and mortality: "though they were gods by office, they were but men, and should die like men." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm

---

## v. 2 — "No, in your hearts you devise injustice…"

- **Heart and hands:** The sin is internal first, then external. Gill: "The heart of man is wickedness itself; it is desperately wicked, and is the shop in which all wickedness is wrought." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm
- **"Weigh out violence":** Ellicott notes the antithesis — instead of weighing justice in the balance, these judges weigh out violence. The image is of deliberate, calculated wrongdoing. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/58.htm
- Spurgeon: "As righteous judges ponder the law, balance the evidence, and weigh the case, so the malicious dispense injustice with malice aforethought in cold blood." — cited in Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- Pulpit Commentary: "Instead of carefully meting out justice to men, after accurately weighing it in the balance of right and equity, you weigh out to them mere wrong and 'violence.'" — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm

---

## v. 3 — "The wicked are estranged from the womb…"

- **Traditional Reformed/Baptist reading (original sin):** Gill says this "original corruption of nature accounts for all the wickedness done by men: they are conceived in sin, shapen in iniquity, and are transgressors from the womb." He adds they are "alienated from God" from birth. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm
- Spurgeon: "No sooner born than alienated from God — what a condition to be found in! … To be untruthful is one of the surest proofs of a fallen state, and since falsehood is universal, so also is human depravity." — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps058.php
- Guzik (Enduring Word): "David understood this of all humanity including himself (Psalm 51:5)." Kidner is cited: the description "is close enough to what is quoted in Romans 3:10ff. to warn the reader that he faces a mirror, not only a portrait." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/

- **Alternative reading (Anglican/older critical):** The Pulpit Commentary explicitly disagrees: "This is the language of hyperbole, and is certainly not the profession of the doctrine of original sin." It says the psalmist means that those who become heinous sinners usually show evil tendencies from childhood — implying others have better dispositions. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm
- Bible.org (Evangelical): "Estranged from the womb … this is eastern hyperbolic imagery, not theology." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-58

**Denominational difference:** Reformed and Baptist teachers (Gill, Spurgeon, Guzik) read v. 3 as teaching original sin / total depravity. The older Anglican Pulpit Commentary and the evangelical Bible.org study guide caution against reading it as a doctrinal statement, calling it hyperbole or "eastern hyperbolic imagery." This reflects a genuine difference in how Protestant traditions handle the verse's relationship to systematic theology.

---

## v. 4 — "Their venom is like the venom of a snake…"

- **Poisonous words:** Gill connects this to Romans 3:13 ("the poison of asps is under their lips"). The lies of these judges are not harmless; they are venomous, infectious, and deadly. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm
- Guzik: "The words of judges and rulers have special power to oppress others, and their poison is more deadly." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- **The deaf cobra:** The Pulpit Commentary explains the adder was "supposed to be deaf, on account of its being very difficult to charm. It was thought obstinately to set itself against the charmer, and, as it were, stop its ears against him." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm
- Bible.org notes the Hebrew word for "charmed" (lit. "whisper") refers to snake charmers. "The people of the ANE thought the sound of a flute (or voice) quieted a snake but today we know it was the rhythmic movement of the flute itself, not the sound." The theological thrust: these judges wilfully refuse to listen to God. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-58

---

## v. 5 — "refusing to hear the tune of the charmer…"

- **Wilful deafness:** Gill stresses the adder "is not deaf naturally, otherwise it would have no need to stop its ear, but of choice." The wicked are "wilfully deaf to all good counsel and advice given them." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm
- Spurgeon: "Ungodly men are not to be won to right by arguments the most logical, or appeals the most pathetic. … It is not in your music, but in the sinner's ear that the cause of failure lies, and it is only the power of God that can remove it." — cited in Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- **Serpent-charming in the ancient Near East:** The Pulpit Commentary notes serpent charmers are alluded to in Ecclesiastes 10:11 and Jeremiah 6:17, and have "at all times been common in the East." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm

---

## v. 6 — "O God, shatter their teeth in their mouths…"

- **Imprecatory prayer:** The psalm shifts from description to direct prayer for judgment. Guzik: "David prayed that God would take vengeance on these dangerous judges. The power of serpents and lions was in their fangs; David asked God to take away their deadly bite." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- VanGemeren (cited in Guzik): "The imprecatory nature of the prayer may seem strange to our ears, but the radical nature of evil requires a response from the God of justice." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- **Serpent-charming imagery:** The Pulpit Commentary explains: "Serpent charmers sometimes, when they have caught their snake, proceed to beat out the poison fangs with a stone or stick." The psalmist alludes to this, then changes metaphor to the young lion. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm
- **Teeth as words:** Gill suggests "their teeth in their mouth" may mean "their malicious words, calumnies, and detractions; teeth being the instrument of speech." Breaking them prevents the mischief. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm
- **"Young lions":** Gill identifies Saul as "the old lion" and his princes, nobles, and courtiers as "the young ones." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm

### On Imprecatory Psalms Generally (Reformed views):

- Ligonier (Reformed): W. Robert Godfrey and others argue Christians can and should pray imprecatory prayers. "We never curse our enemies. We curse God's enemies." Imprecations are "directed against the enemies of God and His purposes, and of His people." Yet "almost always in relation to an imprecation, is a prayer for repentance, so that the enemies are not just cursed." The curse comes "on those who refuse to repent." — https://www.ligonier.org/posts/can-i-pray-imprecatory-prayers and https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ask-ligonier/how-should-christians-view-the-imprecatory-psalms
- The Gospel Coalition (Reformed/Evangelical): "Psalm 58 is not that different than the prayer prayed by the souls of the martyrs in Revelation 6." They note: "The psalmist does not say: 'Help me slay my enemies' … they leave all in the hand of God." The imprecatory psalms "foretell the wrath of God" and "remind us of the punishment we have been saved from by the cross of Jesus Christ." — https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/ad-fontes/christians-unhitch-imprecatory-psalms/

---

## v. 7 — "May they vanish like water that runs off…"

- **Water imagery:** Gill notes several possible meanings: let their courage fail (Josh 7:5); let them be unstable and never settled (Gen 49:4); let them come to nought; let their ruin be swift and irrecoverable as spilled water (2 Sam 14:14). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: "Let them waste away, and go to naught, like water, that runs off and accomplishes nothing." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm
- **Blunted arrows:** Bible.org says the Hebrew idiom is uncertain but "seems to refer to their unjust verdicts and accusations." Either the enemies' weapons become ineffective, or God's arrows cut them down. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-58
- Pulpit: "Let the arrows be as though snapped in two, or headless." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm

---

## v. 8 — "Like a slug that dissolves in its slime, like a woman's stillborn child…"

- **The snail/slug:** Pulpit Commentary: "Snails in Palestine, during dry seasons, often shrink, shrivel up, and disappear from their shells." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm
- Guzik cites Boice: "A slug does not actually melt away as it moves along the ground leaving its slimy trail behind. But it seems to." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- **The stillborn child:** Guzik: "With a severe and startling image, David prayed for the death of his enemies, or rather that they had never been born to see the light of day." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- Bible.org notes a textual problem: "The parallelism between 'snail' and 'a miscarriage' is faulty, but how is uncertain." NIDOTTE suggests "snail" be understood as "a miscarriage." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-58
- Gill: "As a snail when it comes out of its shell liquefies, drops its moisture … and melts away, and dies: so the psalmist prays that everyone of his enemies might die in like manner." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm

---

## v. 9 — "Before your pots can feel the burning thorns…"

- **A famously difficult verse:** The Pulpit Commentary calls it "difficult and obscure" and gives several scholarly renderings: Cheyne translates it as raw flesh in pots being swept away before cooking; the Revised Version speaks of thorns (green and burning alike) being taken by a whirlwind; Kay renders it about raw flesh and hot fury. "The general meaning seems to be that before the wicked judges can enjoy the fruits of their wickedness, the fierce wrath of God will come upon them like a tempest." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm
- Bible.org: "The basic point is that the needed heat for the cooking pot is blown away before it can heat the food (i.e., even fast-starting kindling)." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-58
- Guzik: "The Hebrew of these lines is difficult but the thought may be that David considered how quickly a bunch of dry thorns burn in a fire under cooking pots. David prayed that God's judgment would come upon his enemies like a flash of fire." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- Gill: "Before a pot could be heated with a blaze of thorns … sudden destruction … God takes them away as with a whirlwind … when in health and full strength." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm

---

## v. 10 — "The righteous will rejoice when they see they are avenged…"

- **Rejoicing at judgment:** The Pulpit Commentary states: "As the good man is pained when he sees the ungodly prosper, so he cannot but feel a certain satisfaction and pleasure when punishment overtakes him." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm
- Maclaren (cited by Guzik): "If it is right in God to destroy, it cannot be wrong in His servants to rejoice that He does. Only they have to take heed that their emotion is untarnished by selfish gratulation, and is not untinged with solemn pity for those who were indeed doers of evil, but were themselves the greatest sufferers from their evil." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- G. Campbell Morgan (cited by Guzik): "It is a sickly sentimentality and a wicked weakness that have more sympathy with the corrupt oppressors than with the anger of God." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- **"Wash their feet in the blood":** Bible.org calls this "ANE hyperbole for military victory (cf. Ps. 68:23)." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-58
- Gill: This "denotes the great destruction of the wicked, and the abundance of blood that shall be shed … and the entire victory the saints shall have over them, and their security from them." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm
- Guzik notes that Kidner observes: "The New Testament will, if anything, outdo this language in speaking of the day of reckoning (e.g. Revelation 14:19f.; 19:11ff.), while repudiating carnal weapons for the spiritual war (Revelation 12:11)." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- **Caveat from the Pulpit Commentary:** "It is observable that David, personally, was too indulgent, rather than too severe, towards offenders" — the psalm expresses righteous longing for divine justice, not personal vindictiveness. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm

---

## v. 11 — "Surely there is a reward for the righteous! Surely there is a God who judges the earth!"

- **Universal recognition:** Guzik: "David desired the world to see there was a moral order under God where righteousness is rewarded and wickedness is judged. He longed for the justice that these wicked rulers denied." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- Spurgeon (cited by Guzik): "All men shall be forced by the sight of the final judgment to see that there is a God, and that he is the righteous ruler of the universe. Two things will come out clearly after all – there is a God and there is a reward for the righteous." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-58/
- **"Reward" as "fruit":** Gill notes the Hebrew word means "fruit." The reward is "not of debt as due to them … but of grace, streaming through the blood and righteousness of Christ." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm
- **"A God that judgeth" — plural form:** Gill observes the Hebrew text has a plural ("gods that judge"), which some Jewish interpreters (Kimchi, Ben Melech) say is for honour, or refers to angels (Aben Ezra). Gill sees it as "expressive of a trinity of Persons in the Godhead, Father, Son, and Spirit." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/58.htm
- Bible.org (NET Bible view): The plural participle is "a plural of majesty, referring to YHWH's righteous judgment." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-58
- Pulpit Commentary: "Elohim is joined with a plural here, because the speakers are men generally, not only Israelites." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/58.htm

---

## Summary of Key Tradition-Specific Differences Found

| Issue | Reformed / Baptist | Anglican / Older Critical |
|-------|-------------------|--------------------------|
| **v. 3 and original sin** | Teaches original sin / total depravity (Gill, Spurgeon, Guzik) | Hyperbole, not doctrinal (Pulpit Commentary); "eastern hyperbolic imagery" (Bible.org) |
| **Imprecatory prayers (vv. 6-10)** | Affirmed as proper for Christians; directed against God's enemies; paired with prayer for repentance (Ligonier, TGC) | Acknowledged as proper expression of zeal for divine justice, noting David's personal history of restraint (Pulpit) |
| **v. 11 plural "gods that judge"** | Plural of majesty referring to YHWH (NET Bible); or Trinitarian hint (Gill) | Plural because speakers are all mankind, not only Israelites (Pulpit); or plural of majesty (Bible.org) |

---
